title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

title: Competing Effects Modulate the Rate of Poly(A) RNA Deadenylation in a Biomolecular Condensate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The unique solvent milieu found in biomolecular condensates can control cellular enzymatic reactions and shift reaction kinetics by modulating reactant concentrations, structural dynamics, and enzyme activities. Here, we explore the interplay of multiple regulatory factors within a condensate to control poly(A) RNA deadenylation, the first and rate-limiting step in mRNA turnover. The deadenylase CNOT7, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex, localizes to protein- and RNA-rich granules and shows increased degradation activity in vitro in condensates formed by the C-terminal low-complexity disordered region of CAPRIN1, a component of many ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules. We use a combination of enzymatic assays, kinetic modeling, microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations to deconvolute and define the components that underlie this enhancement. We found that enzyme and RNA are concentrated in condensates relative to buffer, which increases CNOT7 activity, while the equilibrium between CNOT7’s active and inactive states remains unchanged. The concentration-dependent increase in enzymatic rates is counterbalanced by a decrease in the enzyme’s catalytic efficiency, likely due to slower diffusion of CNOT7 and RNA within the condensates, which lessens the probability of enzyme–substrate complex formation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal CNOT7-CAPRIN1 interactions that rely on conserved CAPRIN1 sequence features, hinting at an evolutionarily conserved role for CAPRIN1 condensation. With this quantitative kinetic analysis, we describe the multifaceted mechanism behind regulation of CNOT7 deadenylation by a condensate environment.

title: Mechanically Tunable Quantum Transport in Graphene Nanoribbons with Antiaromatic Motifs
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nonbenzenoid graphene nanoribbons provide a versatile platform for tailoring electronic structures beyond conventional benzenoid π-conjugated systems, yet the impact of their topology on quantum transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate electrical conductance through suspended ladder phenylene nanoribbons containing antiaromatic four-membered rings using scanning tunneling microscope lifting spectroscopy. As the nanoribbon is progressively detached from the substrate, differential conductance measurements reveal successive charge-state transitions accompanied by alternating Kondo resonances, demonstrating the dynamic generation of localized spins in an intrinsically closed-shell nanoribbon. Density functional theory calculations show that the antiaromatic topology reduces the HOMO–LUMO gap and induces a pronounced length dependence of the occupied frontier orbitals, which shift progressively toward and eventually across the electrode Fermi level with increasing suspended length, driving successive charge-state transitions. The transport behavior is quantitatively described within a double-barrier tunneling framework incorporating charge quantization and many-body interactions. These results suggest an antiaromaticity-driven mechanism for charge-state evolution and propose antiaromaticity as a molecular design principle for controlling charge and spin states in nonbenzenoid carbon nanostructures.

title: Interfacial Fueling with Physical Autocatalysis Programs Transient Crystallization and Nonconventional Fluorescence
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chemically fueled self-assembly generates transient structures, but coupling spatially controlled product formation to phase evolution remains challenging, particularly for crystallization. Here we introduce a two-phase interfacial fueling strategy in which a hydrophobic anhydride fuel forms an oil phase and reacts with an aqueous precursor to generate amphiphiles locally at the oil–water interface. In the micelle-forming regime, the resulting assemblies enhance interfacial fuel transport and promote further amphiphile formation, establishing physical positive feedback. Coupling this process to ester hydrolysis enables transient micellar assembly. Decreasing product solubility redirects the same fueling network toward transient crystallization. In this regime, poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) shifts the apparent crystallization boundary and regulates crystal growth and aggregation, with nuclear magnetic resonance titration and molecular simulations supporting polymer–amphiphile association. An alternative anionic polymer partially reproduces aggregation suppression, indicating that this behavior is not exclusive to a single polymer. Counterion-dependent fluorescence provides a label-free optical readout of transient crystallization. Across the tested anhydride–ester systems, these results establish a design framework linking fuel partitioning, product solubility, and intermolecular association to transient structural and optical responses. Extension to other chemical systems requires compatible phase behavior and a suitable balance between product-generation and deactivation kinetics.

title: A Bioinspired Gold–Chalcogen Bonding Synergistic Catalysis Platform: Switchable Activation and Dynamic Functional Group Sampling
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Enzymes achieve exceptional catalytic efficiency by leveraging proximity effects and cooperative interactions, inspiring the design of artificial catalysis systems. However, mimicking this concept has been constrained by rigid activation modes and limited functional group interactions. Inspired by chalcogen-bonding metalloenzymes, we report the design and application of a synergistic gold–chalcogen bonding catalysis platform featuring switchable activation centers and dynamic functional group sampling. This platform employs a rationally designed bifunctional gold–chalcogen bonding catalyst, in which the activation center switches between chalcogen and gold sites, while the complementary moiety provides proximity effect. Chalcogen bonding enables dynamic functional group sampling that allows the catalyst to orthogonally interact with various functional groups, including similar ones such as alkenes and alkynes, thereby triggering unique reactivity. Proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that this platform enables the direct synthesis of sterically hindered ethers via alcohol addition to multisubstituted alkenes, including fully substituted variants. Moreover, this strategy extends to new polymerization reactions of tryptamine and alkyne derivatives via a cyclization pathway. Control experiments confirm that none of these transformations proceed under gold or chalcogen bonding catalysis alone, underscoring the unique and synergistic nature of this platform. Given its high activity and broad potential, the concept of chalcogen-bonding metal synergistic catalysis is expected to find broad applications in developing diverse reactions.

title: Revised Biosynthetic Pathway of Alnumycin Involves a Complex Interplay of Redox Reactions, Stereoisomerization, and an Atypical DUF6081 Isomerase
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Alnumycin A is an antimicrobial natural product distinguished by an unusual 1,3-dioxane moiety attached to an aromatic polyketide core. While previous studies had established that d-ribose serves as the precursor to the 1,3-dioxane and its attachment to the aromatic ring system is catalyzed by a C-glycoside synthase, less is known about its subsequent transformation. Aln6 is a member of the domain of unknown function (DUF) 6081 protein family and was previously annotated as a cofactor-free oxidase. Herein, Aln6 is shown to catalyze a redox-neutral isomerization that converts the ribose moiety to a fused furan-dioxolane via an unprecedented rearrangement mechanism. Aln4 subsequently catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reductive ring-opening of the furan, setting the stage for nonenzymatic rearrangement of the dioxolane that produces the 1,3-dioxane structure and explains the stereochemical diversity of alnumycin A observed in vivo. Together, these findings not only revise the established view of the late-stage biosynthesis of alnumycin A but also redefine the chemistry of Aln6, expanding the catalytic repertoire of the DUF6081 family beyond canonical oxidative reactions.

title: Geometry-Programmed Connectivity Enables Predictive Assembly of Diamond-Family Colloidal Crystals
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The predictive assembly of open colloidal crystals requires encoding specific connectivity rules into building blocks that are otherwise isotropic and lack inherent directionality. Here we introduce a geometry-programmed connectivity strategy in which spatial confinement, rather than surface patterning or lattice templating, programs not only particle coordination but also the accessible bonding arrangement that governs network connectivity. We implement this concept using tetrahedral DNA origami frameworks that confine DNA-functionalized spherical particles and restrict their accessible bonding pathways to four tetrahedrally arranged patches, thereby converting isotropic colloids into effective tetravalent building blocks with geometrically prescribed connectivity. A geometric hard-contact model translates these confinement-defined connectivity rules and the linker-defined interaction range into coordination regimes and lattice symmetry, yielding a predictive phase diagram. Guided by this model, we experimentally realize diamond-family colloidal crystals featuring the coexistence of cubic diamond and double diamond phases, as well as zinc blende and double zinc blende phases. Photonic band-structure calculations predict that the experimentally realized cubic diamond and zinc blende topologies can support complete PBGs in the deep-ultraviolet regime. We thus establish a predictive form of colloidal topological engineering, in which confinement geometry programs local connectivity and selects emergent crystal topology.

title: Programmable Directional Assembly of Hydrogen-Bonded Lead Organic Chalcogenolates
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Controlling the directional assembly of metal organic chalcogenolates (MOCs) with atomic precision remains a synthetic challenge yet represents a critical step toward advancing their programmable syntheses and property investigations. Herein, we present a “hydrogen-bond-directed assembly” strategy to drive the formation of single-crystalline, hydrogen-bonded lead organic chalcogenolates (H-LOCs), offering an ideal platform for elucidating their structure–property relationships. By strategically functionalizing thiophenol with regiochemically or electronically distinct substituents, we achieved precise control at the ligand–ligand interface, yielding six distinct H-LOC architectures mediated by interlayer, intralayer, or cooperative hybrid hydrogen-bonding interactions. These programmed hydrogen-bonding interactions play an essential role in crystal growth, enabling the formation of large single crystals of two-dimensional (2D) LOCs. Combined structural and optical characterizations reveal a linear correlation between the ligand electronic effects and optical bandgaps of the materials, culminating in a narrow bandgap of 1.55 eV for the most electron-donating substituent. Most importantly, the reversible nature of these interfacial hydrogen bonds endows the H-LOCs with excellent solution-processability, allowing them to be fabricated into highly stable films with ambient durability exceeding two months─thereby unlocking their potential for optoelectronic devices.

title: Glycosaminoglycans Promote Amyloid-β Aggregation via Multivalent, pH-Dependent Interactions
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are polyanionic polysaccharides that colocalize with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer’s disease, yet their mechanistic contribution to aggregation remains unclear. Here, we show that GAGs function as pH-responsive electrostatic scaffolds that selectively accelerate Aβ(1–42) aggregation under mildly acidic, early endosomal-like conditions but not at neutral pH. Combining experimental and computational approaches, we identify protonated N-terminal histidines as key determinants of GAG binding. Weak interactions between GAGs and the charged N-terminal region of Aβ promote conformational rearrangements that bring peptides into proximity and expose adjacent hydrophobic aggregation-prone segments, thereby facilitating peptide clustering. Kinetic analyses reveal that aggregation is enhanced in a way consistent with an apparent increase in effective peptide concentration, accelerating nucleation without altering the dominant aggregation pathway. Systematic variation of GAG chain length and sulfation level further demonstrates that aggregation enhancement requires a threshold degree of multivalency, consistent with a clustering-driven mechanism. Together, these findings establish a framework in which pH-dependent polyelectrolyte interactions act as molecular triggers of amyloid nucleation and define the physicochemical parameters that govern when GAGs transition from passive interaction partners to active promoters of Aβ aggregation, providing insight into how cellular microenvironments may regulate the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease pathology.

title: A Cationic Ruthenium Olefin Metathesis Catalyst Supported on Weakly Coordinating Silica
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Silica functionalized with Lewis acidic silylium aluminate ion-pairs ([iPr3Si][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (RF = C(CF3)3)) abstract chloride from the second-generation Grubbs-Hoveyda catalyst (SIMes)Cl2Ru=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4) (GH-II) to form supported [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (1) and iPr3SiCl. Solid-state NMR measurements at 100 K, desorption of Ru from the support, and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy (XAS) are consistent with formation of a monomeric Ru-benzylidene cation that is electrostatically immobilized on the modified silica surface. 1 is active and selective in ring closing metathesis (RCM), self-metathesis, ring opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), acyclic diene metathesis (ADMET), cross metathesis, and ethenolysis reactions. 1 is generally more active than cationic [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)]2[BArF4]2 (GH-II+; BArF4 = tetrakis(3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)borate) in these reactions and gives higher yields with higher selectivity than neutral GH-II under equivalent conditions. DFT calculations comparing models of GH-II+ and 1 suggest that cationic Ru=CH2+ is stabilized by interactions with the anion and accounts for the increase in reaction rates observed using 1 compared to GH-II+.

title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

title: Charge-to-Mass Ratio Regulation of Solvated Li+ Clusters for Ultrafast-Charging Lithium Battery Electrolytes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Extreme fast charging of high-energy lithium batteries is limited by coupled Li+ transport, interfacial desolvation, and electrode degradation. Here, we introduce q/Mcluster as a composition-derived prescreening descriptor, where q is the assigned charge number of the Li-centered carrier (+1 here) and Mcluster is the abundance-weighted composition mass of the cationic clusters in the four most populated solvent-separated ion-pair (SSIP) configurations. A higher q/Mcluster identifies a lower average cluster composition mass and prioritizes electrolyte candidates for transport and electrochemical testing. Guided by this descriptor, we develop a methyl acetate/fluoroethylene carbonate (MA/FEC) electrolyte that favors MA-rich solvated Li+ clusters with lower composition mass and dynamic ligand exchange, while FEC supports interphase stabilization. Simulations and experiments show weaker Li+–solvent association, a lower calculated cluster ligand-removal energy, and faster Li+ diffusion in the optimized formulation. It enables stable operation for 1000 cycles at 15C and 500 cycles in a 1 Ah pouch cell under 3C charging. Composition and cross-family controls support complementary roles for MA-regulated solvation and FEC-derived interphase stabilization, while revealing limits to a single-parameter ranking. Thus, q/Mcluster helps prioritize formulations for independent transport, interfacial, and electrochemical validation.

title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

title: Bright-Field-Hidden Disordered Atomic Textures for Physically Unclonable Functions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical physical unclonable functions (PUFs) relying on unique microscopic randomness serve as a root of trust for advanced hardware security. However, existing optical PUFs typically rely on disordered structural features at the hundred-nanometer or micrometer scale, facing increasing threats from rapidly advancing 3D nanoprinting technologies. Here, we exploit the atomic-scale thickness irregular texture formed during the epitaxial growth of semiconductor thin films as unclonable nanofingerprints, which demand subnanometer-level precision in the vertical direction for any cloning attempt. Such atomic textures are optically stealthy under bright-field microscopy due to their extremely low thickness. To address this, metallic nanofilms are deposited on the semiconductor surface, enabling the visualization of the patterns via surface plasmonic scattering at the metal nanostep edges under dark-field optical microscopy. The proposed PUF offers advantages, including compatibility with semiconductor fabrication processes, high randomness encoding capacity, bright-field concealment, and strong resilience against physical replication. Based on this PUF, we propose a multilevel key scheme applicable to various application scenarios, demonstrating significant application potential in high-security fields, such as device anticounterfeiting, traceability, information encryption, and authentication.

title: Quantifying Effective van der Waals Interactions Across Two-Dimensional Material Interfaces
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Van der Waals (vdW) interactions play a central role in determining the properties and functionality of two-dimensional (2D) materials and their heterostructures. However, quantitative nanoscale characterization of these interactions remains challenging. Here, we introduce a universal multifrequency atomic force microscopy (AFM) framework for quantitative mapping of effective vdW interaction landscapes and the extraction of effective Hamaker constants with Ångström-scale vertical resolution. Using graphene, graphene oxide, hexagonal boron nitride, molybdenum disulfide, and highly oriented pyrolytic graphite as model systems, we systematically investigate the influence of layer number, substrate, defects, step edges, surface roughness, and functionalization on local vdW interactions. The measurements reveal pronounced spatial variations and nonadditive behavior, demonstrating that effective Hamaker constants can be enhanced or suppressed by nanoscale structural and interfacial features. This work provides a rapid and versatile approach for nanoscale characterization of vdW interactions and offers new opportunities for engineering interfacial forces in 2D materials and van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Synergistic Catalysis at the Ni3Te2–Ni3C Heterointerface: Accelerating Water Dissociation for Efficient and Robust Hydrogen Evolution in Alkaline Water and Seawater
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is kinetically limited by sluggish interfacial water dissociation and the subsequent hydrogen intermediate conversion, making the cooperative regulation of consecutive HER elementary steps crucial for achieving efficient electrocatalysis. However, most reported HER heterostructures primarily rely on global electronic structure modulation, while function-oriented interfacial regulation of distinct reaction steps remains insufficiently explored. Herein, a Ni3Te2–Ni3C heterostructure electrode was in situ fabricated on nickel foam via a one-step electrodeposition strategy and systematically evaluated for HER in both alkaline freshwater and alkaline seawater. Mechanistic investigations indicate that Ni3C promotes interfacial water activation and dissociation, whereas the Ni3Te2–Ni3C heterointerface further optimizes the kinetics of hydrogen intermediate conversion, thereby enabling the cooperative regulation of consecutive HER elementary steps. In situ Raman spectroscopy, together with density functional theory (DFT) calculations, provides supportive evidence for the facilitated water dissociation and optimized hydrogen intermediate conversion at the heterointerface. Benefiting from such functional complementarity, the optimized Ni3Te2–Ni3C/NF electrode requires overpotentials of only 26 and 32 mV to achieve 10 mA cm–2 in 1 M KOH and alkaline seawater, respectively, while maintaining good stability under the investigated operating conditions. This work establishes a structure–interface–activity relationship and provides a reaction pathway-oriented design principle for developing efficient alkaline HER electrocatalysts.

title: Decoupling Electrochemical Performance from External Pressure via Mechanically Interlocked 3D Interfaces for Ultra-low-pressure Supercapacitor Pouch Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Supercapacitor pouch cells typically require substantial external stack pressure (typically >2 MPa) to maintain intimate internal interface contact. However, the heavy packaging modules introduce significant inactive mass, reducing system-level energy density. Herein, we report a two-step aligned 3D imprinting strategy that fundamentally decouples electrochemical performance from external compression. By engineering a mechanically interlocked structure, the compaction force is precisely directed toward the interfaces between the active particles, as well as between the particles and the current collector. This prevents lateral slippage, achieving ultra-low internal electrode resistance and conformal interface contact. Consequently, compared with planar electrodes, imprinted electrodes exhibit a 14.3-fold lower interfacial resistance and a 2.7-fold lower equivalent series resistance even under 0.3 MPa stack pressure, delivering an unprecedented average power density of 285 kW kg–1 at 1 mg cm–2 and 28.4 kW kg–1 at 5 mg cm–2. Notably, pouch cells based on 3D-D electrodes sustain 100,000 cycles with 99% capacitance retention, benefiting from the mechanically stabilized interface and the suppressed resistance evolution. Furthermore, this paradigm is compatible with roll-to-roll manufacturing processes, providing a versatile and scalable approach for the next generation of high-power, lightweight, and ultra-low-pressure supercapacitor systems.

title: Carboxylic Acid-Based Hole Transport Layer with Both Anchoring and Passivation in Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The hole transport layer (HTL) plays a pivotal role in the performance of inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs), especially in carrier transport, anchoring to the substrate as a buried interface, and defect passivation. Novel HTLs that simultaneously achieve indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate anchoring, passivation of buried perovskite defects, and favorable interfacial energy alignment are seldom addressed. In this work, we designed a novel HTL (denoted as TPCOOH), which is functionalized with dicarboxylic acid groups in the central phenyl ring, which can anchor onto ITO substrates and passivate the top perovskite, as well as coupling with methylthio-substituted triphenylamine and thiophene units to generate suitable energy alignment and transfer the hole, realizing both passivation and anchoring effects. TPHex, as a control, had dihexyl substitution in the center. Inverted PSC devices based on TPCOOH and TPHex as hole transport layers (0.1 cm2) achieved power conversion efficiencies of 24.68% and 23.72%, respectively. The improved efficiency of TPCOOH-based devices is attributed to suppressed nonradiative recombination, rapid interfacial charge transfer, and minimal energy loss due to well-matched energy levels. These improvements are ascribed to the carboxyl groups in TPCOOH, which anchor to ITO, thus ensuring better film coverage and improved charge transport, while the passivation functionality simultaneously mitigates perovskite defects. Notably, the TPCOOH and TPHex devices retain 75% and 65% of their initial power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) after 1200 h of thermal aging at 65 ± 5 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere.

title: Quantum predator-prey cycles in dissipative Rydberg array
abstract: The predator-prey cycle is a paradigmatic example of self-organized population oscillations in far-from-equilibrium systems, yet testing its underlying mechanism in natural ecosystems is often precluded by uncontrollable microscopic parameters. Here, we propose a quantum analogue of predator-prey dynamics using a tunable two-dimensional Rydberg atom array. Through mean-field analysis and large-scale numerical simulations based on the open-system discrete truncated Wigner approximation, we demonstrate stable predator-prey cycles of Rydberg excitations on microsecond timescales. We show that nonperturbative quantum coherence drives spontaneous time-translation symmetry breaking, leading to globally synchronized oscillations under short-range interactions. Even under desynchronization caused by quantum jumps, locally synchronized predator-prey cycles persist, with amplitude scaling inversely with the square root of the system size. Our work extends the study of predator-prey models to the quantum realm and advances quantum simulation strategies that leverage engineered many-body nonequilibrium effects.

title: Self-evolving Embodied AI
abstract: Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an intelligent system formed by agents and their environment through active perception, embodied cognition, and action interaction. Existing embodied AI remains confined to human-crafted setting, in which agents are trained on given memories and construct models for given tasks, enabling fixed physical embodiments to interact with relatively static environments. Such methods fail in in-the-wild setting characterized by variable physical embodiments and dynamic open environments. This paper introduces self-evolving embodied AI, a new paradigm in which agents operate based on their changing physical embodiment and environment through five software-level components, namely memory self-updating, task self-switching, environment self-prediction, embodiment self-adaptation, and model self-evolution, together with a hardware-level component for physical embodiment evolution, aiming to achieve continually adaptive intelligence through software-hardware co-evolution. Specifically, we present the definition, framework, components, mechanisms, roadmap, and evaluation indicators of self-evolving embodied AI, systematically review state-of-the-art works for realized components, discuss practical applications, and point out future research directions. We believe that self-evolving embodied AI enables agents to autonomously learn and interact with environments in a human-like manner and provides a new perspective toward general artificial intelligence.

title: Aptamers enable a distinct mode of conformational DNA recognition
abstract:
Abstract
                  Watson–Crick base-pairing defines the classical paradigm of nucleic-acid interactions, but growing research reveals noncanonical modes beyond this framework. Here we uncover a mode of interactions by which two DNA strands associate through a ligand-induced conformational rearrangement. Upon binding a small molecule, a structure-switching primary aptamer folds into a conformation that exposes a previously inaccessible docking interface. An independently evolved secondary aptamer recognizes this interface primarily through noncanonical interactions rather than sequence complementarity, reporting the ligand-bound state of the primary aptamer. This interaction is conformation-sensitive: single base-pair changes in the primary aptamer modulate secondary aptamer recognition. Across four chemically distinct small-molecule targets—serotonin, dopamine, testosterone and deoxycorticosterone 21-glucoside—secondary aptamers were identified for three, and the serotonin system was translated into surface-based sandwich assays. These results demonstrate that a ligand-induced conformational state, rather than sequence complementarity or the chemical identity of the ligand, can serve as the epitope for nucleic-acid recognition, expanding the molecular features that DNA can be evolved to detect.

title: A binuclear copper enzyme platform for enantioconvergent radical (pseudo)halogenation
abstract: Despite their intriguing native metalloenzymology, naturally occurring copper enzymes remain underexploited for new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions. Here we report the systematic investigation and reprogramming of natural copper enzymes to catalyse unnatural free-radical (pseudo)halogenation reactions with high enantioselectivity. Evaluation of Cu enzymes in the decarboxylative azidation of redox-active esters revealed activity across multiple copper enzyme families, with type III binuclear copper enzymes, particularly Bacillus megaterium tyrosinase (BmTyr), exhibiting superior activity and enantioselectivity towards both stabilized and unstabilized alkyl radicals after further engineering. The strong halide binding affinity of the binuclear copper system also enabled challenging enantioconvergent bromination, chlorination and isothiocyanation reactions that remained inaccessible to repurposed non-haem iron enzymes. Electron paramagnetic resonance and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopic analyses confirmed the coupled binuclear nature of wild-type and engineered bacterial tyrosinases and provided insight into the origin of their enhanced activity. Collectively, this study establishes binuclear copper enzymes as a powerful platform for new-to-nature stereoselective radical reactions, expanding the scope of metalloenzyme catalysis beyond mononuclear systems. The image explains the catalytic activity of the binuclear copper enzyme tyrosinase from Bacillus megaterium with mutations V218A and N205M. The enzyme contains two copper ions each coordinated by three histidine residues. The enzyme acts on a substrate with two chiral centers labeled R superscript L and R superscript S. On the left, the substrate with an azide group (N3) attached to the R superscript S center is shown as a reactant. On the right, the product has a substituent labeled X, which can be chlorine, bromine, or thiocyanate, attached to the R superscript S center. The enzyme catalyzes the substitution of the azide group by X at the R superscript S position.

title: Memory-Enhanced Visible-Light Photonic Synapses in Interface-Engineered ZnON/IGZO Oxide Transistors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Zinc oxynitride (ZnON) thin-film transistors (TFTs) are attractive visible-light photoactive devices owing to their narrow and tunable optical bandgap; however, the limited population of deep-level trap states can restrict post-illumination carrier retention, resulting in weak photonic synaptic retention. Here, memory-enhanced visible-light photonic synapses are demonstrated using interface-engineered ZnON/Indium gallium zinc oxide (IGZO) double-layer oxide TFTs. A thin IGZO capping layer is integrated onto the ZnON channel to preserve ZnON-dominated red, green, and blue (RGB) photoresponse, while modifying the interfacial electronic environment and carrier-relaxation dynamics. The ZnON/IGZO TFT exhibits RGB responsivities of 2.93, 11.0, and 17.6 A W–1 and specific detectivities of 1.10 × 1012, 3.82 × 1012, and 6.08 × 1012 Jones under red, green, and blue illumination, respectively. The device also exhibits enhanced short- and long-term synaptic retention behavior under pulsed optical stimulation, wavelength-dependent synaptic plasticity, and analogue synaptic weight modulation. Spectroscopic ellipsometry and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveal that the IGZO capping layer preserves ZnON-dominated visible-light absorption, while inducing changes in oxygen-related bonding environments across the bilayer structure. Photoinduced current transient spectroscopy reveals a redistribution of electrically active trap states toward both relatively shallow- and deep-level regions after IGZO capping. The shallow-level states are correlated with enhanced photoresponse, whereas the deep-level states are consistent with delayed carrier relaxation and prolonged post-illumination retention. These results demonstrate that ZnON/IGZO bilayer engineering provides an effective strategy for coupling broadband visible-light sensitivity with tunable carrier-retention dynamics in oxide photonic synapses.

title: A Sequentially Disassembling Nanocomposite Hydrogel with Lesion-Triggered Luteolin Release for Multitarget Acne Vulgaris Therapy
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Acne vulgaris (AV) remains challenging to treat due to antibiotic resistance, side effects, and the lack of topical formulations that concomitantly eradicate Cutibacterium acnes, resolve inflammation, and restore redox homeostasis. Here, we report a sequentially pH-disassembling nanocomposite hydrogel (TCL2.16‰@PQ; PQ represents poly(vinyl alcohol)/quaternized chitosan (PVA/QCS)) for comprehensive AV management, in which tannic acid/Cu2+/luteolin metal–phenolic network nanoparticles (TCL NPs) serve as both drug reservoirs and physical crosslinking nodes within PVA/QCS (PQ) matrix. The hydrogel optimally disassembles at pH 6.5, followed by TCL NP disassembly at pH 6.0, enabling microenvironment-triggered release of luteolin preferentially at the AV lesion site (5.0–7.5, 6.35 ± 1.30; healthy individuals: 4.1–5.8). This design enhances skin permeation flux by 1.5-fold compared to TCL NPs alone. Additionally, the hydrogel's shear-thinning and thixotropic properties make it easy to spread and adhere to the skin. In vitro, the hydrogel completely eradicates Cutibacterium acnes and reduces biofilm biomass by 7.6-fold at 0.2 g/mL, polarizes macrophages to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and scavenges reactive oxygen species through direct radical scavenging and upregulation of SOD/GPx/HO-1. In a murine AV model, the hydrogel achieved complete bacterial eradication and lesion resolution within 14 days, significantly outperforming a commercial metronidazole gel by concurrently reducing inflammation and restoring redox homeostasis. This work establishes a microenvironment-responsive, multitarget nanocomposite platform addressing the core pathogenic factors of AV, presenting a promising alternative to conventional therapies.

title: Open-Air Fabricated Pseudo-Planar Heterojunction Organic Solar Cells with Improved Efficiency and Thermostability via Suppression of Interfacial Degradation
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Boosting both photovoltaic performance and long-term stability is currently the main challenge for organic solar cells (OSCs). In this regard, adopting a pseudo-planar heterojunction (PPHJ) photoactive layer is a promising solution because of its favorable vertical phase distribution; however, it is subject to the limitation of donor/acceptor (D/A) interfacial degradation. Herein, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) is introduced as a multifunctional donor additive, enabling the suppression of interface degradation in the PPHJ photoactive layer and thereby improving the efficiency and thermostability of devices. Specifically, the introduction of PVDF slightly enhances the molecular packing and dielectric property of the photoactive layer, leading to reduced exciton binding energy (Eb) and enhanced charge transport capability of the materials. These improvements stabilize the interfacial morphology and thus suppress interfacial degradation, including deposition-induced and aging-induced degradation. Moreover, PVDF’s hydrophobicity improves moisture tolerance, enabling reliable open-air fabrication of the photoactive layer under high humidity. As a result, the open-air fabricated OSCs achieve an impressive efficiency of 19.24% with enhanced storage stability and thermal stability, which is one of the highest efficiencies for open-air fabricated OSCs. This work highlights the importance of suppressing interfacial degradation in improving performance and stability of PPHJ OSCs and provides a promising strategy to address it.

title: Defect Passivation via a Bifunctional Guanidinium Sulfamate Ligand for High-Efficiency Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Achieving high crystallinity and low defect density remains a critical bottleneck for maximizing the power conversion efficiency (PCE) and operational stability of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Herein, we introduce guanidinium sulfamate (GASM) as a bifunctional ligand to modulate the defect chemistry of perovskite films. DFT calculations reveal thermodynamically favorable binding of GASM to defect sites on selected α-FAPbI3 (100) surface models. Separately, the stronger (100) diffraction response observed by XRD is consistent with improved film crystallinity, although a change in out-of-plane texture cannot be excluded. Meanwhile, theoretical and spectroscopic results suggest Pb–O coordination involving the sulfamate moiety and N–H···I hydrogen bonding involving the guanidinium moiety, consistent with the observed defect-passivation effect. The GASM-treated perovskite films show a stronger (100) diffraction response, larger grains, and a longer photoluminescence lifetime. The resulting n–i–p structured PSCs deliver a champion PCE of 24.43%, alongside environmental stability. These results highlight the potential of GASM as an additive for improving perovskite film quality and suppressing defect-assisted nonradiative recombination, contributing to enhanced photovoltaic performance.

title: Drop-to-Drop Transfer of Magnetic Activity: Imparting Significant Heterogeneity and Reactivity to a Drop via Functionality Transfer from Another Drop
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Interactions between nanoparticles (NPs) and liquid drops have been widely utilized to manipulate both drops and NPs. However, achieving their separation without altering the intrinsic state of either component has remained a significant challenge in NP-laden drop systems. In our previous work (ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2024, 16, 64253–64263), we addressed this challenge by extracting magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) from the interior of an MNP-laden drop as a compact aggregate under the influence of an external magnetic field. In the present paper, we develop a technique that enables the seamless transfer of this extracted MNP aggregate from one liquid drop (the source drop) into the interior of a second liquid drop (the receiver drop). Remarkably, the aggregate, which can be tracked throughout the transfer process, is transferred nearly in its entirety, while neither drop undergoes any permanent deformation throughout the process. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a seamless drop-to-drop transfer of NPs, or, more broadly, the transfer of one drop’s functionality to another (here magnetic activity) without permanently altering the morphology of either drop. Beyond facilitating the NP transfer, the process transforms the receiver drop into a heterogeneous system that exhibits a variety of intriguing phenomena. For example, the transferred NPs can self-assemble into either skyscraper-like solid structures or magnetically responsive liquid layers. The nature of these assemblies depends on whether the MNP transfer occurs once or multiple times, and these assemblies display markedly different dynamics when subjected to magnetic fields of varying orientations, as well as oscillating and rotating magnetic fields. Furthermore, the transfer process converts the receiver drop into a highly stable microreactor for chemical reactions, enabling reaction products to form and persist while remaining minimally exposed to external disturbances that could otherwise compromise their stability.

title: Simultaneously Boosting Stability and High-Temperature Performance of Ni-Rich Cathode Materials by a Negative-Thermal-Expansion Fast Ion Conductor
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nickel-rich layered oxide cathodes have attracted extensive attention for high-energy batteries due to their high capacity, but face challenges such as structural instability, mechanical degradation, interfacial side reactions, and thermal runaway. To address these issues, a multiple-benefit strategy is proposed to modify LiNi0.92Co0.03Mn0.05O2 (NCM92) using Li1.1La0.1Zr1.9(PO4)3 (LLZP) featuring both high ionic conductivity and negative thermal expansion through a facile way. The NCM92 modified with 3 wt % LLZP (denoted as LLZP3) exhibits the best electrochemical performance. Compared to pristine NCM92, the Li+ diffusion coefficient and the discharge specific capacity at 10 C are, respectively, increased by 94.2 and 19.9%, while the capacity retention ratios are, respectively, enhanced by 26.0 and 23.4 percentage points after 200 cycles at 25 °C and 60 °C. Meanwhile, the strain after cycling at 60 °C and the released heat when first charged to 4.3 V are reduced by 55.6% and 62.4%, respectively. According to multifarious characterizations, LLZP can significantly improve the Li+ diffusion kinetics of NCM92, alleviate released heat and volume expansion, and suppress microcrack formation and side reactions during charge/discharge cycling. Noticeably, LLZP exhibits anisotropic volumetric contraction via in situ absorbing heat to enhance thermal safety and interfacial stability. It provides a universal and practical approach for developing high-performance energy materials.

title: Aniline–Peroxide-Initiated Cyclodextrin-Containing Monoliths for Scalable PFAS Removal from Water
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are a class of persistent environmental contaminants that cause negative health effects. These health concerns and impending regulations motivate demand for PFAS removal technologies. Such technologies must be capable of high-throughput, continuous-flow operation, and maintaining treatment performance at large-scales in municipal and industrial treatment systems. Many PFAS remediation technologies rely on particle-based sorbents, which are subject to mass-transfer limitations in large-scale flow-through systems that can limit PFAS removal performance. Recently, we introduced monolithic sorbents for PFAS removal based on styrene-functionalized β-cyclodextrin polymers whose porosity can reduce these mass-transfer limitations. The first monolith formulations were prepared by photoinitiating polymerization within flow-through columns, which limited the monolith’s practical scalability. Here, we address this limitation by using a redox initiation process at room temperature, which is compatible with the high internal phase emulsion and enables scalable fabrication across column dimensions. Mercury porosimetry revealed a bimodal pore size distribution and a larger characteristic maximum pore size in the redox-initiated monoliths compared to the monomodal pore size distribution observed in the photoinitiated materials. Chemical composition and batch adsorption performance remained consistent across redox-initiated monoliths scaled to 36 times the original monolith cross-sectional area. Redox-initiated monoliths outperformed photoinitiated monoliths in flow-through columns, showing later breakthrough of the short-chain PFAS, perfluorobutanoic acid. We also evaluated the PFAS removal performance of scaled redox-initiated monoliths in columns of increasing diameters (0.5, 1, and 1.5 cm). Their performance was consistent across scales, indicating that redox-initiated monoliths with larger cross-sectional areas maintain their promising sorption performance.

title: High-Entropy Design of Commensurate Antiferroelectric Ceramics with Superior Energy Storage Performance
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Antiferroelectric (AFE) ceramic dielectrics are imperative for next-generation energy-storage capacitors because of near-zero remnant polarization. In this work, we construct a new high-entropy antiferroelectric ceramic to synergistically optimize dielectric energy storage by reconstructing the commensurate polarization modulation, thereby delivering an ultrahigh recoverable energy density (Wrec) of ∼14.2 J/cm3 at 71 kV/mm while maintaining a high energy efficiency (η) of ∼84%. In addition, the ceramics deliver remarkable fatigue resistance with stable performance over 105 charge–discharge cycles. This study highlights entropy engineering as a powerful framework for designing high-performance AFE energy-storage ceramics and offers insights for the future development of advanced dielectric capacitors.

title: Nanozymes as Heterogeneous Catalysts: In Operando Aggregation and Altered Apparent Substrate Affinity Affect Catalytic Properties and Immunoassay Reliability
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Nanozymes are synthetic nanoscale catalysts that are actively explored as functional replacements for natural enzymes in various applications. Often, the properties and characteristics of enzymes are directly transferred to nanozymes without considering their unique features as nanosized heterogeneous catalysts. In this article, we explore two often-neglected factors: reduced substrate binding and aggregation of peroxidase-mimicking nanozyme particles that occur in operando (i.e., during catalysis or sample incubation). A competitive Langmuir–Hinshelwood model was utilized to evaluate the impact of organic solvent on substrate binding. In operando aggregation of Au@Pt particles was confirmed by visible spectroscopy, dynamic light scattering, and ultramicroscopy. We demonstrate that both reduced substrate binding and aggregation significantly affect the kinetic parameters of nanozyme catalysis, including approximately three-fold decrease of the apparent Michaelis–Menten constant, a six-fold decrease of the maximum reaction rate, and erroneous conclusions regarding activity inhibition. The effect of aggregation was studied in microplate immunoassays and lateral flow immunoassays of Staphylococcal enterotoxin A (SEA). The results demonstrate that aggregation leads to a reduced specific signal (from immunocomplexes of SEA with Au@Pt-mAb) and an increased nonspecific signal (from aggregated Au@Pt), resulting in a lower signal-to-noise ratio. As a consequence, this leads to false-positive results in microplate immunoassays or even ruins lateral flow immunoassay performance. These results confirm that in operando colloidal stability and substrate binding are crucial factors to be considered for the accurate quantification of kinetic parameters and for various bioanalytical applications.

title: Probing Counterion Distribution Around Cationic Metal–Organic Cages by Fluorescence, Analytical Ultracentrifugation, and Molecular Dynamics
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We report a convenient fluorescence-based approach to probe the counterion association around soluble, cationic metal–organic cages (MOCs) in aqueous solution. Two MOCs incorporating tetra-(4-pyridylphenyl) ethylene (TPPE), an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) chromophore, were employed to monitor the spatial distribution and binding of counter-anions across a range of ionic strengths. Alterations in the fluorescence response of the TPPE groups sensitively respond to the changes in their local environment, providing a probe of counterion location and distribution. The results suggest a stepwise counter-anion association mechanism around MOCs: first around the Pt vertices dominated by electrostatic interactions at low counterion-to-MOC ratios, then interacting with the TPPE ligands at higher ratios. Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) results and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations are in good agreement with this proposed two-stage association mechanism and suggest distinct spatial preferences of different anions. This combined experimental–computational strategy provides a broadly applicable method for elucidating counterion distributions and dynamics around charged nanoscale species in solution.

title: Interfacial Origin of Mn Promotion in Ni/AlO x Catalysts for Methane Pyrolysis and Carbon Nanotube Growth
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Commercial deployment of methane pyrolysis (MP) requires H2 to be produced at a high rate while the solid carbon is recovered as a marketable product such as multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs). Various promoters have been explored for Ni-based MP catalysts, including Mn, but the origin of its effect has remained elusive. Here, Ni/AlOx catalysts containing 0 to 5 wt % Mn were used to separate the two roles that Mn plays in activity and stability. The amount of Ni exposed at an oxide boundary correlated with the apparent CH4 reaction order across the series, identifying the Ni–O–Mn perimeter as the site at which CH4 activation is promoted. The same perimeter converted weakly bound NiO into strongly interacting species that resisted encapsulation, linking the rate and the lifetime of the catalyst to a single interface. At 1 wt %, Mn the apparent activation energy fell from 93.9 to 84.2 kJ mol–1, the CH4 reaction order rose from 0.46 to 0.84, and the turnover number increased from 375 to 456 mol C mol Ni–1. At 2 wt %, MnOx began to bury the Ni surface, and above that loading it segregated into a separate phase, so the promotion was lost. Mn also improved the graphitization and conductivity of the MWCNTs formed at the start of the reaction, but this benefit faded as disordered carbon accumulated. Co-feeding H2 suppressed this accumulation and gave MWCNTs with an electrical conductivity comparable to that of commercial material. The benefit of Mn is therefore set by where it resides rather than by how much is added, and both products of MP reach useful quality only when the promoter loading and the reaction conditions are optimized together.

title: Water-Cluster-Expanded Interpenetrated Covalent Organic Frameworks Create High-Affinity Coordination Microenvironments for Efficient Strontium Capture
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The efficient capture of radioactive strontium (Sr2+) from nuclear-contaminated water is of critical importance for environmental safety and public health protection. Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) with multi-interpenetrated architectures offer the potential for multidentate synergistic coordination toward target Sr2+. However, the confined internal environment arising from uncontrolled multi-interpenetration often restricts coordination freedom, while the concomitant reduction in pore size and obstruction of transport channels impose significant kinetic limitations on the adsorption process. Herein, we report a water-cluster-induced framework swelling strategy implemented in our synthesized 3D TB-COF adsorbent. This approach simultaneously establishes a multisource coordination environment that enhances both Sr2+ affinity and selectivity, and expands the pore channels to eliminate transport barriers, reduce mass-transfer resistance, and improve active-site accessibility. The water-expanded TB-COF adsorbent achieves a record-high maximum adsorption amount (qmax = 346.2 mg g–1) and excellent selectivity in simulated nuclear wastewater, alongside outstanding radiation tolerance. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the superior Sr2+ recognition originates from the water-cluster-modulated coordination space constructed by three adjacent networks. This work provides a general design strategy for developing advanced 3D interpenetrated COF adsorbents toward environmental remediation of nuclear contamination.

title: Reordering of Retinal Reactions Underlies Reversal of Proton-Pump Directionality
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Light-driven proton-pumping rhodopsins transport protons either outward or inward across membranes, but the molecular determinants of transport vectoriality remain unclear. An outward proton-pumping rhodopsin from Pseudomonas putida (PspR) was previously converted into an inward pump by substituting only three amino acid residues. Here, time-resolved resonance Raman spectroscopy reveals that wild-type PspR accepts a proton with a 13-cis retinal chromophore, whereas the engineered inward-pumping PspR triple mutant accepts a proton with an all-trans chromophore, as observed in schizorhodopsins. Intermediate mutant analysis shows that D73F/T78C generates an all-trans M intermediate, while previous transport measurements showed that adding T77S further enhances inward-pumping activity. These findings link reversal of proton-pump vectoriality to reordering of retinal reisomerization and Schiff-base reprotonation, suggesting a strategy for engineering transport directionality in microbial rhodopsins.

title: Orbital Discreteness Modulates Electron-Counting Adsorption Trends in Atomically Dispersed Catalysts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Understanding adsorption at atomically dispersed catalytic sites remains a central challenge, as conventional d-band theory fails to describe emerging molecular-like electronic structures in single-atom systems. Here, we identify a unified electronic framework that bridges metallic single-atom alloys and nitrogen-coordinated graphene single-atom catalysts (transition-metal atoms coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in graphene, TM-N4-Gr), connecting band-like and ligand-field-dominated regimes through a common orbital-filling picture. Systematic density functional theory calculations for C, N, and O adsorption show that adsorption-energy minima in both platforms exhibit a common ten-electron-like counting trend across transition-metal dopants. This behavior originates from molecular-orbital-like filling of dopant-adsorbate hybrid states, linking electron-counting behavior in metallic and coordination-stabilized single-atom environments. Crucially, orbital discreteness is identified as an important factor regulating how this electron-counting trend manifests. In TM-N4-Gr systems, localized d states promote more distinct bonding and antibonding states, leading to enhanced sensitivity to electron filling beyond the optimal electron count, whereas metallic hosts induce electronic delocalization that smooths this response. These results establish a unified orbital-filling framework in which adsorption is governed by the interplay between electron counting and orbital discreteness, providing a general physical basis for atomically dispersed catalysis.

title: A Predictive Betaine Organocatalyst Platform for Asymmetric 1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions Enabled by Interaction-Aware Modeling
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric (organo)catalysis remains a longstanding challenge, particularly in systems where stereocontrol is governed by weak, highly flexible, and substrate-dependent noncovalent interactions. In such regimes, simplified transition-state-based DFT analysis can become unreliable due to the presence of multiple low-energy conformations, competing binding modes, and alternative reaction pathways. We introduce a previously unexplored chiral imidazolium/aryloxide betaine organocatalyst platform for asymmetric 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions of CH-acidic imines with maleimides that operates with exceptional efficiency, reaching turnover numbers of up to 3000 while maintaining high enantiocontrol. To overcome the limitations of transition-state-guided catalyst optimization and enable predictive control beyond the limits of mechanistic intuition, we combined combinatorial catalyst-substrate screening with descriptor-based statistical modeling. Analysis of the resulting data set reveals that no single catalyst is universally optimal across substrate space; instead, enantioselectivity is governed by a catalyst-substrate matching effect. The resulting models identify the molecular features associated with selectivity and enable prospective prediction of enantioselectivity for previously unseen catalysts and a structurally distinct substrate class. These findings establish highly productive metal-free azomethine ylide cycloadditions and demonstrate how interaction-aware data-driven models can provide predictive control in complex asymmetric catalytic systems.

title: Coexisting Liquid-, Glassy-, and Crystal-like Phonons in a Crystalline Solid
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract As main states of matter, crystal, glass, and liquid manifest themselves in distinct transverse collective atomic vibrations. In contrast to crystals where transverse phonons are well-defined throughout Brillouin zones, glasses and liquids process such motions in long and/or short wavelength limits, respectively. Considerable efforts have been made to experimentally probe transverse phonon behavior in these highly anharmonic and disordered materials in pursuit of a universal framework for thermal transport. In this work, inelastic neutron scattering on AgCrSe2 single crystals reveals liquid-, glassy-, and crystal-like phonon features along different crystallographic directions. In particular, the liquid-like behavior is attributed to the significant softening and scattering arising from the nesting effect and dynamical atomic disorder while the glassy-like behavior is due to the selective disorder effect. Our findings challenge conventional boundaries between states of matter at the level of atomic dynamics and establish a materials platform for unifying the thermal transport theories across different states.

abstract: All-solid-state sodium batteries (ASSBs) offer high energy density and safety, but conventional solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layers suffer from low efficiency and severe side reactions.
